nodes.statement:
Consider a non-square matrix A in R^{m x n} and its associated block diagonal matrix K in R^{m x n}, as defined in Equation (ref). We describe a procedure to construct squared matrices from A and K regarding the values of varepsilon_{i,j}.

First, for the case where the dimension of the squared matrix is m, i.e., for all i in {1, 2, ..., m}, we select only one column from each a_{i,j}, where j in {1, 2, ..., p_i}. This corresponds to the scenario where, for a given i, exactly one of the corresponding varepsilon_{i,j} != 0, j in {1, 2, ..., p_i}. We can construct N = prod_{i=1}^{m} p_i such squared matrices for both A and K, denoted as [A]^m_{s_i} and [K]^m_{s_i}, respectively, for i in {1, 2, ..., N}.

Second, when the dimension of the squared matrices is less than m, corresponding to the scenario where, for one or more i in {1, 2, ..., m}, varepsilon_{i,j} = 0 for all j in {1, 2, ..., p_i}, we can construct squared matrices of dimension k < m. These are denoted as [A]^k_{s_i} and [K]^k_{s_i}.

These squared matrices are referred to as the square counterparts of the non-square matrices A and K.

nodes.statement: A square matrix A is said to be strictly column diagonally dominant if for each row i, the absolute value of the diagonal element is greater than the sum of the absolute values of the other elements in the same column: |a_{ii}| >= sum_{j > i} |a_{ij}| for all i.

A square matrix $A$ is said to be strictly column diagonally dominant if for each row $i$, the absolute value of the diagonal element is greater than the sum of the absolute values of the other elements in the same column:
\[
|a_{ii}| \geq \sum_{j > i} |a_{ij}| \quad \text{for all } i.
\]

nodes.statement: A matrix A is called strictly column diagonally balanced dominant if there exists a diagonal matrix D such that |AD| + |DA^T| is strictly column diagonally dominant. Furthermore, if all the diagonal elements of AD + DA^T are positive then the matrix A is called positive diagonally balanced dominant.

nodes.statement: For a real nonsquare matrix A in R^{m x n}, if one can find an individual diagonal positive matrix D_i > 0, so that all its m-order squared matrices [A]^m_{s_i} in R^{m x m} satisfy the following LMIs, [A]^m_{s_i} D_i + D_i ([A]^m_{s_i})^T > 0, then, we call the non-square matrix A an individual Volterra-Lyapunov stable matrix.

nodes.statement: Consider m groups of cards, where each group contains p_i distinct cards. A player can place a bet on each combination of m cards, one card from each group. The payoff for a specific combination is denoted as \gamma(\zeta_1, \zeta_2, ..., \zeta_m) > 0. We record the payoff for each card in a constructed combination as (\gamma(\zeta_1, \zeta_2, ..., \zeta_m))/(m). Suppose the player desires a specific ratio \kappa_{kj} > 0 between the j_{th} card of group k and the first card of that group. If the set of payoffs \gamma(\zeta_1, \zeta_2, ..., \zeta_m) satisfies the following conditions, then the player can implement their desired strategy: \gamma_{(1, 1, ..., 1)} = 1 \gamma_{( \zeta_1, \zeta_2, ..., \zeta_{(i-1)}, j, \zeta_{(i+1)}, ..., \zeta_{m})} = \gamma_{( \zeta_1, \zeta_2, ..., \zeta_{(i-1)}, 1, \zeta_{(i+1)}, ..., \zeta_{m})} \kappa_{ij},

The condition \gamma_{(1, 1, ..., 1)} = 1 ensures that the payoff for choosing one card from each group, where all cards are the first cards of their respective groups, is normalized to 1. This establishes a baseline. 2. Ratio Preservation Condition: According to Condition (REF), we easily see that all \gamma(\zeta_1, \zeta_2, ..., \zeta_m) can be set as a positive real value. Then, the payoff of the first card in group k is \frac{1}{m}(\sum_{\zeta_1=1}^{p_1} ... \sum_{\zeta_{k-1}}^{p_{k-1}} \sum_{\zeta_{k+1}}^{p_{k+1}} ... ... \sum_{\zeta_m}^{p_m} \gamma_{( \zeta_1, ..., \zeta_{k-1}, 1, \zeta_{k+1}, ..., \zeta_m )}). \begin{proof}
We will prove the desired strategy can be achieved by constructing a set of payoffs that satisfies the conditions in equation \eqref{sub_sssa}.

1. \textbf{Normalization Condition:} \\
First, according to Condition (\ref{sub_sssa}), we easily see that all $\gamma(\zeta_1, \zeta_2, \cdots, \zeta_m)$ can be set as a positive real value.
The condition $\gamma_{(1, 1, \cdots, 1)} = 1$ ensures that the payoff for choosing one card from each group, where all cards are the first cards of their respective groups, is normalized to 1. This establishes a baseline.

2. \textbf{Ratio Preservation Condition:} \\
According to Condition (\ref{sub_sssa}), we easily see that all $\gamma(\zeta_1, \zeta_2, \cdots, \zeta_m)$ can be set as a positive real value.
Then, the payoff of the first card in group $k$ is
$$
\frac{1}{m}(\sum_{\zeta_1=1}^{p_1} \cdots \sum_{\zeta_{k-1}}^{p_{k-1}} \sum_{\zeta_{k+1}}^{p_{k+1}} \cdots \cdots \sum_{\zeta_m}^{p_m} \gamma_{( \zeta_1, \cdots, \zeta_{k-1}, 1, \zeta_{k+1}, \cdots, \zeta_m )}).
$$
The payoff of the $j_{th}$ card in group $k$ is
\begin{equation}\label{eq_meili}
\begin{aligned}
&\frac{1}{m}(\sum_{\zeta_1=1}^{p_1} \cdots \sum_{\zeta_{k-1}}^{p_{k-1}} \sum_{\zeta_{k+1}}^{p_{k+1}} \cdots \cdots \sum_{\zeta_m}^{p_m} \gamma_{( \zeta_1, \cdots, \zeta_{k-1}, j, \zeta_{k+1}, \cdots, \zeta_m )})\\
=&\frac{1}{m}(\sum_{\zeta_1=1}^{p_1} \cdots \sum_{\zeta_{k-1}}^{p_{k-1}} \sum_{\zeta_{k+1}}^{p_{k+1}} \cdots \cdots \sum_{\zeta_m}^{p_m} \kappa_{k j} \gamma_{( \zeta_1, \cdots, \zeta_{k-1}, 1, \zeta_{k+1}, \cdots, \zeta_m )}).\\
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
Thus, the second equation of Condition (\ref{eq_meili}) ensures that the payoff for choosing the $j_{th}$ card of group $k$ in combination with other cards is directly proportional to the payoff for choosing the first card of that group, with the ratio being $\kappa_{kj}$.

%By defining the payoffs according to these conditions, you can construct a set of payoffs that allows the player to implement their desired strategy. This strategy involves placing bets based on the ratios $\kappa_{kj}$ to achieve the desired proportions of cards from each group, while the normalization condition ensures a consistent reference point for payoffs.
\end{proof}

nodes.statement: Considering that A is a simultaneous Volterra-Lyapunov stable matrix, the following inequality should be true: [A]^m_{s_i} D + D ([A]^m_{s_i})^T > 0. Assume the total number of the m_{th}-order squared matrices [A]^m_{s_i} is N, i.e., i \in \{1,2, ..., N\}. Based on inequality (REF), we can conclude, for any \gamma_i>0, i \in \{1, ..., N\}, the following inequality holds (\gamma_1 [A]^m_{s_1} + \gamma_2 [A]^m_{s_2} ... + \gamma_N [A]^m_{s_N})D + D (\gamma_1 [A]^m_{s_1} + \gamma_2 [A]^m_{s_2} ... + \gamma_N [A]^m_{s_N})^T >0 Based on Lemma REF, for any diagonal positive matrix D > 0 and j \in \mathcal{M}, we have Re\{ \sigma [ (\sum_{i=1}^{N} \gamma_i [A]^m_{s_i}) D]_j \} >0. Without loss of generality, we only consider the proof for the m_{th}-order matrices. So, we omit the subscript j in the following discussions. According to structure of K, as before, we redefine the sub-indices of the n columns of A as follows: A=[\boldsymbol{a}_{1,1}, ..., \boldsymbol{a}_{1,p_1}, \boldsymbol{a}_{2,1}, ..., \boldsymbol{a}_{2,p_2}, ..., ..., \boldsymbol{a}_{m,1} ...,\boldsymbol{a}_{m,p_m}]. Correspondingly, we redefine the sub-indices of \gamma_i>0, i \in \{1, ..., N\} in inequality (REF) as follows; \gamma_{(\zeta_1, \zeta_2, ..., \zeta_m)}, where \zeta_i \in \{1,2,...,p_i\}. The coefficient \gamma_{(\zeta_1, \zeta_2, ..., \zeta_m)} means from each of the following group of vectors to select one vector to correspond to a term \gamma_{(\zeta_1, \zeta_2, ..., \zeta_m)} [A]^m_{s_i} in inequality (REF): Group 1: \boldsymbol{a}_{1,1}, ..., \boldsymbol{a}_{1,p_1}, Group 2: \boldsymbol{a}_{2,1}, ..., \boldsymbol{a}_{2,p_2}, ..., ..., Group m: \boldsymbol{a}_{m,1} ...,\boldsymbol{a}_{m,p_m}. Further assume D=diag\{[d_1,d_2,..., d_m]\}. Then the core part of the equation (REF) can be expressed as follows: (\sum_{i=1}^{N} \gamma_i [A]^m_{s_i}) D =[ d_1 ( \sum_{j=1}^{p_1} (\sum_{\zeta_2=1}^{p_2} \sum_{\zeta_3=1}^{p_3} ... \sum_{\zeta_m}^{p_m} \gamma_{( j, \zeta_2, ..., \zeta_m )} ) \boldsymbol{a}_{1,j} ), d_2 ( \sum_{j=1}^{p_2} (\sum_{\zeta_1=1}^{p_1} \sum_{\zeta_3=1}^{p_3} ... \sum_{\zeta_m}^{p_m} \gamma_{( \zeta_1, j, \zeta_3, ..., \zeta_m )} ) \boldsymbol{a}_{2,j} ), ... ... ... d_m ( \sum_{j=1}^{p_m} (\sum_{\zeta_1=1}^{p_1} \sum_{\zeta_2=1}^{p_2} ... \sum_{\zeta_{(m-1)}}^{p_{(m-1)}} \gamma_{( \zeta_1, \zeta_2, ..., \zeta_{(m-1)},j)} ) \boldsymbol{a}_{m,j} ) ]. On the other hand, the matrix AEK can be expressed as AEK = [ \sum_{j=1}^{p_1} \varepsilon_{1j} k_{1j} \boldsymbol{a}_{1,j}, \sum_{j=1}^{p_2} \varepsilon_{2j} k_{2j} \boldsymbol{a}_{2,j}, ..., \sum_{j=1}^{p_m} \varepsilon_{mj} k_{mj} \boldsymbol{a}_{m,j}] = [ \sum_{j=1}^{p_1} \tilde {k}_{1j} \boldsymbol{a}_{1,j}, \sum_{j=1}^{p_2} \tilde {k}_{2j} \boldsymbol{a}_{2,j}, ..., \sum_{j=1}^{p_m} \tilde {k}_{mj} \boldsymbol{a}_{m,j}] = [ \tilde {k}_{11} \sum_{j=1}^{p_1} \frac{\tilde {k}_{1j}}{\tilde {k}_{11}} \boldsymbol{a}_{1,j}, \tilde {k}_{21} \sum_{j=1}^{p_2} \frac{\tilde {k}_{2j}}{\tilde {k}_{21}} \boldsymbol{a}_{2,j}, ..., \tilde {k}_{m1} \sum_{j=1}^{p_m} \frac{\tilde {k}_{mj}}{\tilde {k}_{m1}} \boldsymbol{a}_{m,j}] = [ \tilde {k}_{11} \sum_{j=1}^{p_1} \bar {k}_{1j} \boldsymbol{a}_{1,j}, \tilde {k}_{21} \sum_{j=1}^{p_2} \bar {k}_{2j} \boldsymbol{a}_{2,j}, ..., \tilde {k}_{m1} \sum_{j=1}^{p_m} \bar {k}_{mj} \boldsymbol{a}_{m,j}]. In the above equation, \tilde {k}_{ij} = \varepsilon_{i,j} k_{i,j} \ge 0, and \bar {k}_{ij} = \frac{\tilde {k}_{i,j}}{\tilde {k}_{i,1}} (considering the case \tilde {k}_{i,1} \ne 0), which implies \bar {k}_{i1}=1. Thus, we can conclude, that for any non-negative diagonal matrices E \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}, the inequality (REF) is always satisfied.

Based on inequality (REF), we can conclude, for any \gamma_i>0, i \in \{1, ..., N\}, the following inequality holds (\gamma_1 [A]^m_{s_1} + \gamma_2 [A]^m_{s_2} ... + \gamma_N [A]^m_{s_N})D + D (\gamma_1 [A]^m_{s_1} + \gamma_2 [A]^m_{s_2} ... + \gamma_N [A]^m_{s_N})^T >0 Based on Lemma REF, for any diagonal positive matrix D > 0 and j \in \mathcal{M}, we have Re\{ \sigma [ (\sum_{i=1}^{N} \gamma_i [A]^m_{s_i}) D]_j \} >0. Without loss of generality, we only consider the proof for the m_{th}-order matrices. So, we omit the subscript j in the following discussions. According to structure of K, as before, we redefine the sub-indices of the n columns of A as follows: A=[\boldsymbol{a}_{1,1}, ..., \boldsymbol{a}_{1,p_1}, \boldsymbol{a}_{2,1}, ..., \boldsymbol{a}_{2,p_2}, ..., ..., \boldsymbol{a}_{m,1} ...,\boldsymbol{a}_{m,p_m}]. Correspondingly, we redefine the sub-indices of \gamma_i>0, i \in \{1, ..., N\} in inequality (REF) as follows; \gamma_{(\zeta_1, \zeta_2, ..., \zeta_m)}, where \zeta_i \in \{1,2,...,p_i\}. The coefficient \gamma_{(\zeta_1, \zeta_2, ..., \zeta_m)} means from each of the following group of vectors to select one vector to correspond to a term \gamma_{(\zeta_1, \zeta_2, ..., \zeta_m)} [A]^m_{s_i} in inequality (REF): Group 1: \boldsymbol{a}_{1,1}, ..., \boldsymbol{a}_{1,p_1}, Group 2: \boldsymbol{a}_{2,1}, ..., \boldsymbol{a}_{2,p_2}, ..., ..., Group m: \boldsymbol{a}_{m,1} ...,\boldsymbol{a}_{m,p_m}. Further assume D=diag\{[d_1,d_2,..., d_m]\}. Then the core part of the equation (REF) can be expressed as follows: (\sum_{i=1}^{N} \gamma_i [A]^m_{s_i}) D =[ d_1 ( \sum_{j=1}^{p_1} (\sum_{\zeta_2=1}^{p_2} \sum_{\zeta_3=1}^{p_3} ... \sum_{\zeta_m}^{p_m} \gamma_{( j, \zeta_2, ..., \zeta_m )} ) \boldsymbol{a}_{1,j} ), d_2 ( \sum_{j=1}^{p_2} (\sum_{\zeta_1=1}^{p_1} \sum_{\zeta_3=1}^{p_3} ... \sum_{\zeta_m}^{p_m} \gamma_{( \zeta_1, j, \zeta_3, ..., \zeta_m )} ) \boldsymbol{a}_{2,j} ), ... ... ... d_m ( \sum_{j=1}^{p_m} (\sum_{\zeta_1=1}^{p_1} \sum_{\zeta_2=1}^{p_2} ... \sum_{\zeta_{(m-1)}}^{p_{(m-1)}} \gamma_{( \zeta_1, \zeta_2, ..., \zeta_{(m-1)},j)} ) \boldsymbol{a}_{m,j} ) ]. On the other hand, the matrix AEK can be expressed as AEK = [ \sum_{j=1}^{p_1} \varepsilon_{1j} k_{1j} \boldsymbol{a}_{1,j}, \sum_{j=1}^{p_2} \varepsilon_{2j} k_{2j} \boldsymbol{a}_{2,j}, ..., \sum_{j=1}^{p_m} \varepsilon_{mj} k_{mj} \boldsymbol{a}_{m,j}] = [ \sum_{j=1}^{p_1} \tilde {k}_{1j} \boldsymbol{a}_{1,j}, \sum_{j=1}^{p_2} \tilde {k}_{2j} \boldsymbol{a}_{2,j}, ..., \sum_{j=1}^{p_m} \tilde {k}_{mj} \boldsymbol{a}_{m,j}] = [ \tilde {k}_{11} \sum_{j=1}^{p_1} \frac{\tilde {k}_{1j}}{\tilde {k}_{11}} \boldsymbol{a}_{1,j}, \tilde {k}_{21} \sum_{j=1}^{p_2} \frac{\tilde {k}_{2j}}{\tilde {k}_{21}} \boldsymbol{a}_{2,j}, ..., \tilde {k}_{m1} \sum_{j=1}^{p_m} \frac{\tilde {k}_{mj}}{\tilde {k}_{m1}} \boldsymbol{a}_{m,j}] = [ \tilde {k}_{11} \sum_{j=1}^{p_1} \bar {k}_{1j} \boldsymbol{a}_{1,j}, \tilde {k}_{21} \sum_{j=1}^{p_2} \bar {k}_{2j} \boldsymbol{a}_{2,j}, ..., \tilde {k}_{m1} \sum_{j=1}^{p_m} \bar {k}_{mj} \boldsymbol{a}_{m,j}]. In the above equation, \tilde {k}_{ij} = \varepsilon_{i,j} k_{i,j} \ge 0, and \bar {k}_{ij} = \frac{\tilde {k}_{i,j}}{\tilde {k}_{i,1}} (considering the case \tilde {k}_{i,1} \ne 0), which implies \bar {k}_{i1}=1. Now, according to Lemma REF, in Equation (REF), if we let d_i = \tilde{k}_{i1} (i \in \{1,2,...,m\}), and \gamma_{(1, 1, ..., 1)} = 1 \gamma_{( \zeta_1, \zeta_2, ..., \zeta_{(i-1)}, j, \zeta_{(i+1)}, ..., \zeta_{m})} = \gamma_{( \zeta_1, \zeta_2, ..., \zeta_{(i-1)}, 1, \zeta_{(i+1)}, ..., \zeta_{m})} \bar{k}_{ij}, the left-hand side of Equation (REF) equals that of Equation (REF). Thus, we can conclude, that for any non-negative diagonal matrices E \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}, the inequality (REF) is always satisfied.

nodes.statement: For a proper and asymptotically stable non-square system H(s) in C^{m x n}, we define its steady state transfer matrix as A=H(0) in R^{n x m}. If there exists a block diagonal non-square matrix K in C^{n x m} such that for all non-negative diagonal matrices E in R^{n x n}, and j in M, Re{ sigma_i ( [A E K]_j ) } >0, where M is the index set consisting of k tuples of integers in the range 1,...,m, and Re{ sigma_i(M) } represents the real part of the i-th eigenvalue of matrix M, then the nonsquare system can be controlled by a distributed integral controller and achieve Decentralized Unconditional Stability.
